rows.claim_text: Drop-and-hook turn time cut from 48 minutes to 24 minutes, gate to gate, at a Primo Brands site, in a field-validated side-by-side pilot (both arms instrumented and timed in parallel, same gate, same trucks, same days).
rows.scope: Primo Brands only; do not imply this result at any other named or unnamed account.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Primo Brands cut drop-and-hook turn time from 48 to 24 minutes, measured in a side-by-side pilot, now running network-wide across their live sites.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Every truck at Primo's live sites turns in half the time it used to, 24 minutes instead of 48, same gate, same trucks, no new concrete poured.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not drop 'measured'/'at Primo' and imply a generic or guaranteed result. Do not restate as '50% more volume shipped' (the 50% is a TIME reduction, not a volume increase).
rows.source_excerpt: "48 to 24 min / Drop-and-hook turn, gate to gate / Measured in a side-by-side pilot: both arms instrumented, then rolled network-wide." (yardflow.ai/proof/); canon.py: "48 min -> 24 min gate-to-gate (MEASURED, Primo)."

rows.claim_text: The driver-journey layer (flowDRIVER/flowBOL check-in and paperless custody protocol) is live at 24 Primo Brands sites (plants and DCs), running the same driver journey and clocks.
rows.scope: Primo Brands only. '24 sites' = driver-journey deployment count, not YardFlow's total customer count and not Primo's total committed network (that is 260, see CR-007).
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: 24 sites live on one protocol at Primo Brands.
rows.provocative_phrasing: 24 Primo Brands plants and DCs now run the same driver check-in and paperless custody protocol, wall to wall, on the same clock.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not say '24 sites' when you mean the 260-site committed network. Do not say 'live at every Primo site' (only 24 of 260 are live).
rows.source_excerpt: "24 sites / live on one protocol / Plants and DCs across the US, running the same driver journey and the same clocks." (yardflow.ai/proof/)

rows.claim_text: flowYMS (full yard-management-system orchestration: dock assignment, live yard status, move dispatch) is deployed at 10 of Primo Brands' 24 live driver-journey sites; the driver journey and eBOL layer runs at all 24 independent of full YMS orchestration.
rows.scope: Primo Brands only. This is the load-bearing distinction between 'driver journey live' (24) and 'full YMS live' (10) — do not collapse the two.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: flowYMS is deployed at 10 of Primo's 24 live sites; the driver-journey layer runs at all 24.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Primo runs full YMS orchestration at 10 sites today, with the other 14 driver-journey sites next in line for the same YMS.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not say 'flowYMS is live at 24 sites' or 'the full YMS is live at Primo' without the 10-of-24 qualifier.
rows.source_excerpt: "the driver journey is live at 24 Primo Brands sites, and flowYMS is deployed at 10 of those 24." / footnote 13: "Driver journey live at 24 sites; flowYMS deployed at 10 of those 24."

rows.claim_text: Sites running the driver-journey layer at Primo Brands shipped about 5% more volume (realized production capacity) than comparable sites without the layer, on the same dock-office headcount, observed.
rows.scope: Primo Brands, driver-journey layer alone (not the full YMS stack). An observed comparison, not a controlled trial and not a guarantee.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: About 5% more volume, observed, from the driver-journey layer alone, on flat dock-office headcount.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Primo's dock offices shipped 5% more freight on the same headcount the moment the driver-journey layer went live, before the YMS was even switched on.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Never '5%+ at every location/facility/site' or 'everywhere' (canon.py hard-blocks this pattern). Never attribute the 5% to the full YMS or to automation. Never call it 'measured' with the same rigor as the 48->24 pilot; the correct word is 'observed'.
rows.source_excerpt: "~5% / Production capacity gained / More volume shipped on flat headcount, measured on the driver-journey layer alone." (yardflow.ai/proof/). canon.py BLOCK rule: 'Overclaim: 5%+ at every location. The +5% is Primo driver-journey, observed.'

rows.claim_text: $1M+ per site in incremental annual profit is YardFlow's conservative MODELED floor, derived from Primo's measured ~5% volume lift priced at real per-truckload margin, not a measured or guaranteed result.
rows.scope: Framed as a modeled floor derived from Primo's economics; extendable to a prospect's network only through the ROI model, never asserted as their number without running it.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: $1M+ per site in incremental annual profit, modeled off Primo's measured economics. A floor, not a ceiling.
rows.provocative_phrasing: The model says standardizing one Primo-scale site is worth $1M+ a year, and that's the floor, not the ceiling.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Never 'measured', 'proven', or 'guaranteed' next to this figure (canon.py MEASURED_CLAIM_RE forbids pairing measured-language with the $1M+ figure). Never present it as a specific prospect's number without running their inputs through the ROI model.
rows.source_excerpt: "It is a conservative modeled floor, not a survey result: a site moving about 5% more volume on the same dock-office headcount and the same dock doors, valued at real margin per truckload... the per-site figure is conservative for the category." (footnote 19)

rows.claim_text: Conservative direct-paper-savings model: $0.05-$0.10/page, 3 pages saved per shipment, 250 shipments/site/day, 260 operating days/year, 24 sites = roughly $234,000-$468,000/year and 4.68 million pages avoided. This is a labeled floor excluding labor, storage, retrieval, disputes, and detention value.
rows.scope: A YardFlow-branded conservative model, always shown with its stated assumptions (shipment counts, operating days, site count). Anchored by a public podcast episode reading these figures aloud; the low end of the range cannot be lowered without Casey + Jake sign-off.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: A YardFlow conservative model: $0.05-$0.10/page, 3 pages saved per shipment, direct paper cost only, roughly $234K-$468K/year at Primo's scale. A floor, not a forecast; full economics live in the ROI model.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Just killing the paper BOL is worth $234K to $468K a year across a 24-site network, and that's before a single minute of labor or detention savings gets counted.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not present as a customer's actual savings without re-deriving from their shipment volume. Do not drop the 'YardFlow conservative model, direct paper only' label. Do not cite the fully-loaded (~$0.70/page) storage-and-retrieval estimate as a fact; it is noted only qualitatively.
rows.source_excerpt: "Formula: 3 pages saved x $0.05-$0.10 x shipments x 260 days x 24 sites. Direct-paper only. Full economics: yardflow.ai/roi." roi-model skill: "Spoken figures ($0.05, 15 cents, $234,000...) are anchored by the 50-min episode and cannot be re-voiced."

rows.claim_text: Primo Brands has committed its entire network, 260 sites under contract, to YardFlow; 24 of those 260 are live today.
rows.scope: Primo Brands only. 260 is Primo's own committed network size and must never be implied of a prospect's network or of YardFlow's total footprint.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Primo Brands committed its entire network, 260 sites under contract, with 24 live today and the rest rolling out.

rows.permitted_external_phrasing: EZ-Pass at the gate, air-traffic control for the trailers.
rows.provocative_phrasing: EZ-Pass at the gate, air-traffic control for the trailers. That's what a yard looks like when it finally runs on data instead of a clipboard.

rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Drivers check in from their phone, no app, no guard, no clipboard.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Drivers check themselves in from their own phone. No app to download, no guard shack, no line.

rows.claim_text: flowBOL (digital custody / eBOL) is a generally available capability: paperless, timestamped bill-of-lading signature and chain of custody, replacing wet-signed paper BOLs.

rows.source_excerpt: "Dock office / flowBOL / Signs the BOL digitally. Paperless, timestamped chain of custody." (yardflow.ai homepage)

rows.claim_text: flowYMS (dock assignment, live dock/yard state, gate and workflow exception handling, spotter/yard-move tasking, trailer-location and trailer-state tracking) is a generally available product capability, deployed in production at 10 of Primo Brands' 24 live sites.
rows.scope: Product capability is GA; production deployment evidence is Primo-specific (10 of 24 sites). Trailer-state/location tracking here refers to the standard YMS orchestration layer, not the camera-based self-mapping RTLS described in CR-017, which is pilot-stage.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: flowYMS assigns the right dock, tracks trailer and yard state live, clears exceptions before they breach, and dispatches yard moves, on one screen.
rows.provocative_phrasing: One screen assigns the dock, tracks every trailer, and clears the exception before it turns into a detention charge.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not conflate this with the camera-based autonomous trailer-mapping capability (flowTWIN self-mapping RTLS), which is a Primo pilot only (see CR-017), not GA.
rows.source_excerpt: "Dock coordinator / flowYMS / Assigns the right door and sees every dock's live state on one screen." (yardflow.ai). Pricing playbook Core bundle: "YMS [trailer orchestration, spotter tasking]".

rows.claim_text: Network standardization (common definitions and KPIs across sites, site scorecards, cross-site comparability, a network rollout playbook, one executive screen across every yard) is a generally available capability, positioned as phase 4 of the YardFlow sequence.
rows.scope: Capability/positioning claim; the only network-scale customer evidence on the pages reviewed is Primo Brands (24 live of 260 committed sites).
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: One screen runs every site; common definitions and KPIs, site scorecards, and cross-site comparability across the network.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Every site reports the same numbers, the same way, so a VP can finally see which of 40 yards is actually the problem instead of guessing from 40 spreadsheets.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not assert network standardization is proven at scale for any account other than Primo without separate evidence.

rows.claim_text: 'Automation readiness' is a sequencing/methodology claim, not an automated capability: YardFlow's published order of operations is driver journey first, digital custody second, YMS orchestration third, network standardization fourth, physical automation last ("automate last is an engineering law").
rows.scope: Methodology/thesis claim, safe everywhere. Never describe 'automation readiness' itself as a delivered automated feature; it describes the state a network reaches after phases 1-4.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: We sequence: driver journey, digital custody, YMS orchestration, network standardization, then physical automation, so automation lands on a network that's actually ready for it.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Buy the robot before you fix the workflow and you've just automated the chaos. Standardize first. Automation is the reward, not the fix.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not say YardFlow 'automates the yard' as a current, generally-available end state for a new customer; automation is explicitly gated behind the first four phases (see CR-016).
rows.source_excerpt: "Driver journey first. Digital custody second. YMS orchestration third. Network standardization fourth. Physical automation after that." / "05 Automate · GATED"

rows.claim_text: Physical automation (machine vision at scale, RTLS, autonomous yard moves, network-wide automation) is explicitly labeled GATED in YardFlow's own published sequence, i.e. roadmap/positioning, not a currently generally-available deliverable for a new customer.
rows.scope: Roadmap/methodology framing is fine to state publicly (it is already on the page). Do not sell it as a deliverable capability for a new deployment.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Physical automation is the last, gated step in the sequence, added once the network is standardized.
rows.provocative_phrasing: YardFlow deliberately holds physical automation until the network is standardized, because a robot dropped into an unstandardized yard just automates the mess faster.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Never claim autonomous physical automation as an out-of-the-box GA deliverable, or imply a new customer gets self-driving yard trucks or fully autonomous spotting on day one.
rows.source_excerpt: "05 / Automate / GATED / Machine vision / RTLS and autonomous moves / Network-wide automation"

rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not publish or send in writing: the incumbent vendor name, the site name, or the contract-expiration detail. Do not describe this pilot as a GA, proven-at-scale capability.

rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Use only as cited: 'Kroger wrote off roughly $2.6 billion unwinding its Ocado robotic-fulfillment bet' etc., always with the cited source (Grocery Dive, CNN Business, Wikipedia, Isaacson's Musk biography).
rows.provocative_phrasing: Kroger just wrote off $2.6 billion automating fulfillment centers before the operating model was ready. The lesson: sequence the workflow before you buy the machine.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Never imply Kroger, Tesla, Adidas, or Webvan are YardFlow customers, prospects in active deals, or otherwise affiliated with YardFlow beyond being cited case studies.
rows.source_excerpt: "Kroger wrote off roughly $2.6 billion unwinding its Ocado robotic-fulfillment bet. Tesla burned through Model 3 production hell over-automating a line before it was simplified. Adidas closed its automated Speedfactories..."

rows.forbidden_phrasing: 'throughput', 'throughput capacity' as the customer-facing benefit.
rows.source_excerpt: canon.py: '"throughput" is retired customer-facing vocab (post-pivot ban).' / 'throughput-capacity: BLOCK, Banned phrase.'

rows.claim_text: Retired metaphor family: 'Volatility Tax' / 'Variance Tax', 'viscosity' (as a customer-facing metaphor), and 'Industrial Fluidity' are retired branding, superseded by the realized-production-capacity thesis.
rows.scope: All outbound and on-site copy; the underlying shader system in the codebase is still internally named 'Variance Tax' for engineering purposes only, which is not a copy concern.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Use 'realized production capacity' framing instead.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: 'Volatility Tax', 'Variance Tax', 'viscosity' (as a value metaphor), 'Industrial Fluidity'.
rows.source_excerpt: canon.py: 'retired-metaphor: BLOCK, Retired metaphor family (Volatility Tax / viscosity / Industrial Fluidity).'

rows.claim_text: Positioning ban: never describe YardFlow as 'not a YMS', or as something that 'coexists with', sits as a 'layer above', or is 'not a replacement/not displacement' for an existing YMS. Post-pivot, YardFlow is pro-YMS and flowYMS is a core module.
rows.scope: All outbound and on-site copy.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: State displacement directly: YardFlow includes and runs the YMS (flowYMS), standardized network-wide.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: 'not a YMS', 'coexist', 'layer above', 'not a replacement', 'not displacement'.
rows.source_excerpt: canon.py: 'not-a-yms: BLOCK, Post-pivot we are PRO-YMS. Never position as "not a YMS".' / 'coexist-layer: BLOCK, Banned displacement-hedge phrasing.'

rows.claim_text: Sales-deck teaser figure referenced on the live homepage: 'Network ROI breakdown ($87.4M across 50 sites, 11.5x legacy YMS)' inside the 13-slide sales-deck description.
rows.scope: This aggregate figure appears only as unfootnoted sales-deck teaser copy on the homepage; unlike the $1M+/site figure (CR-005), it carries no visible derivation, assumptions, or source citation, and it is not consistent by simple arithmetic with the per-site modeled floor (50 sites x $1M+ would be a materially different total). Do not cite in cold outreach until it is derived and footnoted to the same standard as the paper's numbers.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Do not cite this figure externally. If asked about the sales deck's ROI numbers, point to the footnoted $1M+/site and 48->24 figures instead.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: '$87.4M across 50 sites', '11.5x legacy YMS', or restating this as a general YardFlow benchmark.
rows.source_excerpt: "Sales Deck / 13-slide presentation. Network ROI breakdown ($87.4M across 50 sites · 11.5x legacy YMS)..." (yardflow.ai homepage). roi-model skill: "Any dollar figure without a source or a 'modeled' label — there has been a fabrication audit; numbers without provenance get killed."

rows.claim_text: Never lump paper/paperwork into a 'same at every facility' consistency or standardization list; the product eliminates paper, it does not standardize it.
rows.scope: All outbound and on-site copy.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: 'We eliminate the clipboard', 'paper out, fewer people' — kill verbs only.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: 'standardize your paperwork', 'the same paper process at every facility', 'consistent/uniform paperwork'.
rows.source_excerpt: "YardFlow eliminates paperwork, it does not standardize it... the verb should be one of: eliminate, kill, no, drop, ditch. Never 'standardize,' 'consistent,' 'uniform,' 'same.'" canon.py: 'standardize-paper: BLOCK'.

rows.claim_text: Style rule: 'yards' is always plural when referring to the network/thesis-level concept ('the yards are on your radar'); singular 'yard' is reserved for one explicit physical site.
rows.scope: All outbound and on-site copy.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: 'If the yards are on your radar...', 'your yards were never on the network'. Singular is fine only for one named physical site: 'the pilot yard at Conley, GA'.
rows.provocative_phrasing: If you're still talking about 'the yard' like it's one place, you're thinking about the old, single-site YMS. The whole game moved to 'the yards,' the network.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: 'If the yard is on your radar' (singular, network sense) when the network is meant.
rows.source_excerpt: "YardFlow's core differentiation is the network... The plural 'yards' signals the network view that makes us unique." canon.py SINGULAR_YARD: WARN rule flags singular 'yard' in network sense.

rows.claim_text: Named public proof accounts cleared for use: Primo Brands (full proof suite, CR-001 through CR-008) and Kroger (cited only as a third-party automate-last cautionary example per CR-020, never as a YardFlow customer). Direct competitors of Primo Brands (bottled-water rivals: Niagara, Crystal Geyser, CG Roxane, Mountain Valley) are among the MOST qualified prospects and get the full Primo-proof treatment in copy, including the proof metrics (CR-001-CR-008). The only constraints are operational, not copy: (1) never ask Primo itself to give a tour, a reference call, or an intro to one of its own competitors, and (2) never target Primo's own family brands (BlueTriton / Nestle Waters NA) as if they were a separate competitor prospect, since they are Primo itself.
rows.scope: Naming and targeting rule for cold outreach; governs when the Primo proof suite (CR-001-CR-008) may be cited.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Cite Primo Brands' proof metrics in outreach to bottled-water competitors exactly as you would to any other prospect.
rows.provocative_phrasing: The bottled-water rival cutting into Primo's shelf space is running the exact same paper-choked yard problem Primo had, and Primo already proved what fixing it is worth.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not ask Primo to serve as a live reference (tour, call, intro) for a named competitor. Do not treat BlueTriton/Nestle Waters NA as a distinct competitor account; they are Primo Brands.
rows.source_excerpt: "A direct competitor of our live reference customer is one of the MOST qualified prospects, not a disqualified one... The only constraint is the reference-use rule: never ask the reference (Primo) to give a competitor a tour or serve as their named reference/intro. We still pitch the competitor and solve the same problems. Distinct from Primo's OWN brands (BlueTriton / Nestle Waters NA = Primo itself) which are correctly excluded."

rows.claim_text: Only Primo Brands' 48-to-24-minute compression is measured. A prospect's own current gate-to-gate turn time is unknown until asked, but posing the arithmetic of that same compounding across their own daily trucks and sites is a fair, sourced question.
rows.scope: Use only as a question inviting the prospect to supply their own current turn time; never assert or assume their number.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: If your average drop-and-hook runs anywhere near 45 minutes today, what does cutting it in half do to trailer turns across your network, the way it did at Primo's 24 live sites?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not state or assume the prospect's current turn time. Do not say 'you'll cut your turn time in half' as a promise; keep it a question.
rows.source_excerpt: "That is more volume on the same footprint, realized production capacity with no new concrete." (research-paper.ts, line ~869) — the compounding logic behind CR-001's measured 48->24 result.

rows.claim_text: Primo's driver-journey layer alone produced about 5% more shipped volume on flat headcount. Posing that same rate as a hypothetical against a prospect's own volume and margin, explicitly framed as 'if the same rate showed up for you', is a fair question, never a promised result.
rows.scope: Must stay conditional ('if... the same rate Primo produced'); never imply the prospect will or already does see 5%.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: If a 5% capacity lift, the same rate Primo's driver-journey layer produced, showed up in your plant's numbers this year, without a new truck, a new dock, or a new hire, what would that be worth on your P&L?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not drop the 'if' framing and assert the prospect will see 5%. Never say '5% at every site' (see CR-025).
rows.source_excerpt: Derived directly from the sourced facts in CR-004 ("~5%... measured on the driver-journey layer alone", yardflow.ai/proof/) and CR-005 ($1M+/site modeled floor).

rows.claim_text: Primo's published testimonial explicitly ties the volume gain to zero added dock-office headcount. Extending that logic to ask a prospect what flat headcount plus more freight would do to their own cost per shipment is a fair, sourced question.
rows.scope: Never state a specific cost-per-shipment change for the prospect; the number stays open.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Primo took on more volume with the same dock-office headcount. What would flat headcount and more freight moved do to your cost per shipment?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not state or estimate the prospect's cost-per-shipment result.
rows.source_excerpt: Built directly on the published Primo testimonial quoted in CR-008 ("took on additional volume while remaining headcount neutral in the dock office").

rows.claim_text: The paper-savings formula's inputs are all named and public: $0.05-$0.10/page direct cost, 3 pages saved per shipment, and the prospect's own shipments/site/day, operating days/year, and site count are the only unknowns. Inviting a prospect to run their own numbers through the same named formula is a source-backed scenario question, not a claimed result.
rows.scope: Model inputs are named exactly as YardFlow states them ($0.05-$0.10/page, 3 pages/shipment); only the prospect's own shipments/site/day and site count are to be asked for, never guessed on their behalf.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Take 3 pages saved per shipment at $0.05 to $0.10 a page. Run it against your own shipments-per-site-per-day and site count the way we ran it against Primo's 250 shipments/site/day and 24 sites for $234K-$468K a year. What does your version of that formula total?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not fill in a guessed shipments/site/day or site count for the prospect. Do not state a specific dollar total for them without their real inputs.
rows.source_excerpt: Formula named verbatim in research-paper.ts: "Formula: 3 pages saved x $0.05-$0.10 x shipments x 260 days x 24 sites. Direct-paper only."

rows.claim_text: The $1M+/site modeled floor is built from a named formula: about 5% more volume, on flat dock-office headcount and flat dock doors, valued at real margin per truckload. Bottled water (Primo's own product) carries a lower margin than most shipping categories, so the per-site number is conservative for higher-margin freight. Asking what the same formula produces at a prospect's own margin per load is a fair, sourced scenario question.
rows.scope: Never state the prospect's own dollar result without running their actual margin per truckload through the model; the logic (lower margin -> conservative floor) is sourced, the prospect's own number is not.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Primo's $1M+/site number is built on bottled water's own margin per load, one of the lower-margin categories we've modeled. What does the same 5%-more-volume formula produce once we run it against your margin per truckload?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not assert that a prospect's per-site number will definitely be higher than Primo's without actually running their inputs.
rows.source_excerpt: "Bottled water runs lower margin than most shipping categories, so the per-site figure is conservative for the category. Full, buyer-specific derivation is priced against a real network in the ROI model." (footnote 19)

rows.claim_text: Primo expanded from proof at a slice of its network to a 260-site company-wide contract. Asking what evidence a prospect's own leadership would need to make the same expansion decision is a fair, sourced question.
rows.scope: Never imply the prospect has already agreed to, or is close to, a network-wide contract.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Primo didn't stop at a pilot. They put their entire 260-site network under contract on the strength of 24 sites' results. What would your leadership need to see to make the same call?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not imply the prospect is already negotiating a network-wide deal.
rows.source_excerpt: Built on CR-007's sourced fact: "Primo Brands committed its entire network: 260 sites under contract, 24 live today." (yardflow.ai/proof/)

rows.claim_text: The paper states that half of the 48-minute legacy turn was wait time, not physical movement. Asking a prospect what fraction of their own dwell time is wait rather than movement is a fair diagnostic question grounded in that finding.
rows.scope: Never assert the prospect's own wait-to-movement ratio; ask, don't tell.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: At Primo, half of the 48-minute turn was pure wait, gate queue and dispatch lag, not the physical move. How much of your average dwell time is your truck actually sitting still, doing nothing?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not state or assume the prospect's own wait-to-movement ratio.
rows.source_excerpt: "The compression sits in the wait, the gate queue and the dispatch lag, not in the physical move." / "Half the turn time is synthetic capacity, and the half that vanished was wait, not movement."

rows.claim_text: The paper cites ATA data that long-haul truckload driver turnover runs near 90%/year, arguing shorter, less frustrating yard visits are a retention lever. Asking a prospect to value an hour saved at the gate against their own turnover cost is a fair, sourced question.
rows.scope: Never state the prospect's own turnover rate or attribute their turnover directly to yard conditions without evidence.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Long-haul driver turnover runs near 90% a year industry-wide, per the ATA. If the yard is the worst part of a driver's day at your docks, what's an hour saved at the gate worth against what it costs you to replace a driver?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not state the prospect's own turnover rate or assert their yard is the cause of driver attrition.
rows.source_excerpt: "...which matters when long-haul truckload turnover runs near 90% a year (ATA)."

rows.claim_text: The paper documents Kroger's ~$2.6B Ocado write-off and other automate-first failures as consequences of automating before standardizing. Asking a prospect evaluating automation vendors whether their own workflow is standardized enough to avoid the same fate is a fair, sourced diagnostic question.
rows.scope: Frame as a diagnostic question; never assert the prospect's yards are unstandardized.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Kroger wrote off $2.6 billion automating fulfillment centers before the operating model was ready. If a robotics vendor is calling on you right now, is your driver journey and custody data clean enough for that robot to actually compound value, or will it just automate the mess you already have?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not assert the prospect's yards are unstandardized; pose it as a question they answer for themselves.
rows.source_excerpt: Built on the sourced cautionary case studies in CR-020 and the GATED automation sequencing in CR-016.

rows.claim_text: The paper argues a YMS can only orchestrate as well as the arrival, custody, status, seal, and exception events feeding it. Asking a prospect who already owns a YMS whether it is starved of clean inputs is a fair, sourced diagnostic question.
rows.scope: Never assert the prospect's YMS is failing; pose it as a question they answer for themselves.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: A YMS is only as good as what feeds it. If your arrival, custody, and exception events are still late, local, or trapped in a phone call, what is your existing YMS actually orchestrating?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not assert the prospect's YMS is failing or that their events are in fact late/local/incomplete.
rows.source_excerpt: "A YMS cannot orchestrate the yards if the arrival, custody, status, seal, and exception events feeding it are late, local, incomplete, or trapped inside conversations... That is not a software problem. That is an input problem."

rows.claim_text: The paper frames the BOL as a legal contract, receipt, and document of title simultaneously (NMFTA). Asking a prospect what happens in a dispute when they cannot produce a timestamped digital version is a fair, sourced question.
rows.scope: Keep hypothetical; never assert the prospect has had or will have a specific dispute.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: NMFTA calls the bill of lading a contract, a receipt, and a document of title, all three, in one document. When a load gets disputed six months from now, can you produce a timestamped version of any of those three, or just a wet-signed paper copy in a filing cabinet?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not assert the prospect has had, or will have, a specific dispute.
rows.source_excerpt: "NMFTA describes the BOL as a contract between shipper and carrier, a receipt for shipped goods, and a document of title. Digitizing it is not office hygiene. It is custody infrastructure."

rows.claim_text: The paper's network-standardization phase argues common definitions and KPIs are required before sites can be fairly compared. Asking a multi-site prospect whether they can currently identify their worst-performing yard is a fair, sourced question.
rows.scope: Never assert the prospect's sites use inconsistent definitions; ask, don't tell.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: If every site in your network defines 'on time' or 'dwell' a little differently, how would you actually know which of your yards is your worst?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not assert the prospect's sites use inconsistent definitions.
rows.source_excerpt: "04 Standardize / Common definitions and KPIs across sites / Site scorecards and cross-site comparability / The network rollout playbook."

rows.claim_text: The paper's YardFlow Readiness Index weighs driver flow, dock flow, paper flow, spotter flow, exception flow, and automation runway, with paper flow and automation runway weighted heaviest. Asking a prospect to self-rate across those same dimensions before trusting a robot in their yard is a fair, sourced diagnostic question.
rows.scope: Never assign the prospect a specific Readiness Index score without them completing the actual assessment; the weighting logic is sourced, their score is not.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: The paper's Readiness Index weighs paper flow and automation runway heaviest, because they're the data backbone a robot has to read. Where would your yards actually score on driver flow, dock flow, paper flow, spotter flow, and exception flow, before you'd trust them to run a robot?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not assign the prospect a specific score; invite self-assessment only.
rows.source_excerpt: "Paper flow and Automation runway carry weight 3. They are the data backbone a robot reads... Driver flow and Dock flow carry weight 1." (ooo.txt lines ~644-646)

rows.claim_text: Primo Brands committed its entire network after proof from a slice of it. Asking a direct Primo competitor whether they can afford their own yards being the one part of the supply chain still running on paper while a rival standardizes is a fair, sourced competitive question.
rows.scope: Use only with prospects who are legitimate direct competitors of Primo per CR-033's definition (bottled-water manufacturers); never imply Primo endorsed or referred the outreach.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: One of the largest bottled-water networks in the country just put its entire footprint under contract to standardize its yards. If your yards are still running on paper and radios, what's that costing you against a rival who isn't?
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not name Primo directly in a way that implies Primo endorsed reaching out to the competitor, and never claim Primo gave a referral or introduction.
rows.source_excerpt: Built on the sourced facts in CR-007 (260-site commitment) and the competitor-targeting rule in CR-033.

rows.claim_text: The yards are the physical handoff between transportation and warehouse execution, and remain comparatively unmanaged even though warehouses have been optimized and transportation digitized; the paper calls the yard 'the enterprise's physical API,' too often run by 'a person with a clipboard.'
rows.scope: General market observation, safe on any surface.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Warehouses got optimized. Transportation got digitized. The yard, the physical handoff between the two, is still running on a clipboard.
rows.provocative_phrasing: The yards are the enterprise's physical API, and in most networks that API is a person with a clipboard.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not imply this describes a specific named prospect's yards without evidence; keep it a general market observation.
rows.source_excerpt: "The yards are not a parking lot. They are the enterprise's physical API. And in too many networks, that API is a person with a clipboard."

rows.claim_text: 72.7% of supply chain/logistics professionals surveyed are exploring dock and yard automation, but only 12.9% already have a plan to sequence it, per the 2026 State of Dock and Yard Management survey of 149 professionals (C3 Solutions; named once per artifact, then aliased 'the yard survey' per the copy-voice competitor-citation rule).
rows.scope: General market observation, safe on any surface, with the C3 alias rule applied on second and later mentions within the same artifact.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Almost three-quarters of the industry is shopping for yard automation. Fewer than one in eight actually has a plan to sequence it.
rows.provocative_phrasing: 72.7% of the industry wants the robots. 12.9% have a plan. Everyone else is about to buy automation their own yards aren't ready for.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not name 'C3 Solutions' more than once per standalone artifact; alias as 'the yard survey' after first mention (copy-voice rule).
rows.source_excerpt: "72.7% were exploring dock and yard automation, but only 12.9% already had a plan." / "Exploring automation 72.7% / Already have an automation plan 12.9%" (Fig. 01)

rows.claim_text: Inefficient manual processes remain the #1 operational challenge (40.3%) in the same yard survey, ahead of every other named challenge.
rows.scope: General market observation.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Manual process inefficiency is still the single biggest operational headache in dock and yard management, ahead of everything else on the list, per the industry's own survey.
rows.provocative_phrasing: The industry's own survey says manual process inefficiency beats every other challenge, including cost. The basics are still broken.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not present this as if it were measured at any specific named account.
rows.source_excerpt: "Manual process inefficiency, #1 challenge / 40.3%" (Fig. 01, order-of-operations page)

rows.claim_text: 55.7% of the same survey's respondents named implementation effectiveness, not features, support, or price, as the top driver of software satisfaction.
rows.scope: General market observation.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Buyers don't say they regret the feature list. They say they regret the rollout. Implementation effectiveness beats price as the top satisfaction driver in the industry's own survey.
rows.provocative_phrasing: 55.7% of the industry says rollout quality decides whether yard software actually works, not the feature list and not the price.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not imply this is YardFlow's own customer-satisfaction data; it is third-party survey data, cited.
rows.source_excerpt: "55.7% say implementation effectiveness, not features or price, decides whether yard software delivers."

rows.claim_text: 95.7% of survey respondents rate sustainability important or extremely important, and 87.1% say the same of driver experience; the paper ties both to carrier relationships and service reliability, and cites a former Convoy leader's account of carriers rating facilities, with low ratings reflected back in price.
rows.scope: General market observation; the Convoy/GoodShip anecdote is a named, sourced third-party account (The Freight Pod, Episode 85).
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: 95.7% of the industry now rates sustainability as important to their yard strategy, and 87.1% say the same about driver experience. Carriers already rate your facility the way a guest rates a hotel, and a bad rating shows up in what they charge you.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Carriers rate your facility like a hotel guest rates a room, and a bad rating already shows up in your rate confirmation.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not state a specific carrier's rating of a specific named prospect's facility; the sourced example is general (Convoy app ratings, not any named shipper here).
rows.source_excerpt: "Ryan Soskin... has described how Convoy's driver app let carriers rate each facility one to five stars... if carriers do not like going somewhere, that eventually gets 'reflected in the price.'"

rows.claim_text: The paper's central diagnostic is that a YMS can only orchestrate as well as the arrival, custody, status, seal, and exception events feeding it; when those events are late, local, incomplete, or trapped in conversations, the YMS is forced to orchestrate around chaos, which the paper frames as an input problem, not a software problem.
rows.scope: General market/thesis observation; explains why YMS deployments stall industry-wide.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: A YMS deployment doesn't stall because the software is bad. It stalls because it's starved of clean arrival, custody, and exception data, an input problem dressed up as a software problem.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Most YMS deployments that stall aren't broken software. They're starving on the data nobody standardized before turning the system on.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not name a specific YMS vendor or a specific named prospect's deployment as the example.
rows.source_excerpt: "A YMS cannot orchestrate the yards if the arrival, custody, status, seal, and exception events feeding it are late, local, incomplete, or trapped inside conversations."

rows.claim_text: The paper argues automation compounds whatever operating model it lands on: landed on an unstandardized workflow, it inherits the chaos rather than fixing it, producing 'an expensive island of automation that cannot compound across the network.'
rows.scope: General market/thesis observation.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: A robot dropped into a yard that still hands paperwork to a guard doesn't fix the yard. It just automates the mess, one expensive island at a time.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Automation doesn't fix unstandardized yards. It inherits them, and it inherits them at robot prices.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not name a specific automation vendor as an example of this failure mode; the paper's named examples (Kroger/Ocado, Tesla, Adidas, Webvan, see CR-020) are the sourced ones to cite.
rows.source_excerpt: "Automation does not fix unstandardized yards. It inherits them." / "Stack a robot on an analog operation... you get an expensive island of automation that cannot compound across the network. You get tech density, not operational control."

rows.claim_text: NMFTA describes the bill of lading as a contract between shipper and carrier, a receipt for shipped goods, and a document of title simultaneously; the paper argues digitizing it is custody infrastructure, not office hygiene.
rows.scope: General market/thesis observation.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: A bill of lading is a contract, a receipt, and a document of title, all at once, per the industry's own trade group. Leaving it on paper isn't an admin inconvenience, it's an unmanaged legal document.
rows.provocative_phrasing: A wet-signed BOL isn't a paperwork problem. It's a legal document, a contract, and a receipt, sitting unmanaged in a filing cabinet.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not imply NMFTA endorses YardFlow specifically; NMFTA is cited only for the definition of a BOL's legal function.
rows.source_excerpt: "NMFTA describes the BOL as a contract between shipper and carrier, a receipt for shipped goods, and a document of title. Digitizing it is not office hygiene. It is custody infrastructure."

rows.claim_text: The paper frames 'automate last' as an engineering law rather than a slogan, citing Elon Musk's five-step algorithm (question requirements, delete, simplify, accelerate, automate) and his own admission that over-automating the Tesla Model 3 line caused 'production hell.'
rows.scope: General market/thesis observation; the Musk quote is sourced to Walter Isaacson's 2023 biography.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Elon Musk didn't learn this the easy way. He admitted the Model 3 line's 'production hell' came from automating before he'd deleted and simplified the process. Automate last isn't a slogan, it's step five of an algorithm that runs Tesla and SpaceX.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Even Musk automated too early once, and called it his own mistake. Automate last isn't a YardFlow slogan, it's an engineering law he had to relearn the hard way.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not imply Musk or Tesla endorse YardFlow; the citation is for the sequencing principle only.
rows.source_excerpt: "The big mistake was that I began by trying to automate every step. We should have waited until all the requirements had been questioned, parts and processes deleted, and the bugs were shaken out." Elon Musk, on the Tesla Model 3 line. Walter Isaacson, Elon Musk, 2023.

rows.claim_text: DHL Supply Chain's Insight 2030 survey found 44% of operations had deployed warehouse robotics, but only 34% of executives were fully satisfied with the results, an adjacent data point the paper uses to show automation deployment outpacing operational readiness even in the warehouse, not just the yard.
rows.scope: General market observation, adjacent to yards (warehouse robotics), cited to reinforce the sequencing thesis.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: 44% of operations have already deployed warehouse robotics. Only 34% of their executives are fully satisfied with what it delivered. The gap between buying automation and being ready for it isn't unique to yards.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Nearly half of warehouse operators already bought the robots. Two-thirds of their own executives aren't happy with what they got.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not present the DHL figure as YardFlow's own data or as specific to yards rather than warehouses.
rows.source_excerpt: "DHL Supply Chain found 44% of operations had deployed warehouse robotics, and only 34% of executives were fully satisfied with the results." (Insight 2030 Supply Chain Leaders Survey, November 2025)

rows.claim_text: The paper cites ACT Research on trucking capacity structurally tightening (carrier exits, driver constraints, rising spot and contract rates) and argues that as capacity reprices, the cheapest capacity a shipper has is the volume its own yards are currently leaking through wait time.
rows.scope: General market observation.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: Trucking capacity is getting structurally tighter and more expensive, per ACT Research. The cheapest capacity left on the table isn't a new carrier contract, it's the volume your own yards are currently leaking through wait time.
rows.provocative_phrasing: The cheapest truckload capacity in your network right now isn't a new carrier contract. It's the volume your own yards are leaking through wait time.
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not state a specific capacity or rate figure for the prospect's own lanes; the ACT Research citation is a general market trend only.
rows.source_excerpt: "ACT Research reports trucking capacity structurally tightening: carrier exits, driver constraints, and spot and contract rates rising... the cheapest capacity is the kind you already own: the volume your network recovers when the yards stop leaking time."

rows.claim_text: The paper positions network standardization as the phase where value compounds, arguing common definitions, KPIs, and rollout logic across sites turn a single-site win into an enterprise-level comparability advantage.
rows.scope: General market/thesis observation.
rows.permitted_external_phrasing: A single standardized yard is a nice case study. A standardized network is where the value actually compounds, because now you can compare 40 yards on one set of numbers instead of 40 local definitions of 'on time.'
rows.provocative_phrasing: One good yard is a case study. A standardized network is a competitive advantage, because it's the only way to actually compare 40 yards instead of trusting 40 different local definitions of 'on time.'
rows.forbidden_phrasing: Do not imply any specific prospect network is already standardized or already compounding value; this is a general market/thesis point.
rows.source_excerpt: Section title: "Network standardization is where the value compounds." / Fig.03 phase 04: "Common definitions and KPIs across sites / Site scorecards and cross-site comparability."

rows.claim_text: YardFlow's camera-based passive RTLS and gate-vision cameras are live at the Primo Brands (formerly Nestle Waters) plant in Breinigsville, PA, where Primo is retiring an active-tag, puck-based RTLS because the passive camera system is more accurate and scales across sites. The YardFlow team ran a full on-site deployment there at the start of September 2026.
rows.scope: Sales email only. The incumbent (PINC/Kaleris pucks) may be named in sales email; Casey already did so to Target on 2026-06-11 and to Target/Alex Wheeler on 2026-08-18. Do not host on yardflow.ai or in decks without a separate approval. Source: Casey first-person 2026-09-15.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Next door in Breinigsville, Primo Brands is retiring a puck-based RTLS for our passive camera system because it is more accurate and it scales.

rows.claim_text: Three automakers opened yard conversations with YardFlow in the last six weeks: GM's global logistics IT team met with us 2026-08-27 and took a YardFlow demo on 2026-09-16 (Casey: went well); Volkswagen took a call on 2026-09-17 (Casey: went well); Ford is evaluating YardFlow through the L Marks open-innovation program (opened 2026-08-13).
rows.scope: Sales email only. Conversations, demos, evaluations, never customers or pilots won. Re-verify before reuse after 2026-10-15.
rows.provocative_phrasing: GM's global logistics IT team took a YardFlow demo in September and Volkswagen took a call the same week. Ford is running us through its innovation program.

rows.claim_text: First on-site camera deployment at Primo Brands Breinigsville: 24 spotter-cab cameras across 12 spotters, a gate camera and the locally built on-site computer installed in two days (Jake to Target, 2026-09-01: "12 spotters and one gate ... in 2 days"; the next deployment is expected to take under a day); software updates push remotely to the drivers' phones and to the gate.
rows.scope: Sales email. Source: Casey first-person 2026-09-15.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Twenty-four spotter cameras, a gate camera and the on-site computer went in in two days, and updates push remotely to the phones and the gate.

rows.claim_text: Primo Brands plans to pilot the passive camera RTLS and gate-vision system at five more sites in 2027.
rows.scope: Sales email. Planned, not contracted; say plans/is going to, not has signed. Source: Casey first-person 2026-09-15.
rows.provocative_phrasing: Primo plans to pilot it at five more sites in 2027.

rows.claim_text: The machine-vision RTLS and gate system ingests and runs proprietary inference on hundreds of thousands of trailer images and locations a day, and large players including Nestle, GM, Kenco and Lazer have shown interest.
rows.scope: Sales email. Interest, not customers. Source: Jake Koppinger email 2026-09-01.
rows.provocative_phrasing: We are running inference on hundreds of thousands of trailer images a day, and Nestle, GM, Kenco and Lazer have all leaned in.

rows.claim_text: Companies in live conversation with YardFlow in the last 60 days per HubSpot deals and meetings: Nestle, Mondelez, Kraft Heinz, Boston Beer, Ball, Kroger, GXO, NFI, Americold, UACL, Wesco (plus approved GM, Ford, VW, Kenco, Lazer). See PROOF_STACK.md pipeline table.

rows.claim_text: In the 2026-09-16 demo, GM's global logistics IT team said they were excited about the future state once the gap in their yards is closed: their yards produce no structured data today; with YardFlow every gate event, custody handoff and trailer move becomes structured data, and it scales across sites. Specific sites were discussed; the impact is the message.
